post-body:
Quick answer · no carpet to sell you

Five carpet constructions cover almost everything sold in Lynnwood: textured plush, frieze (twist), berber (loop), pattern (cut-and-loop), and saxony. For rooms walked on daily, the safest buy is a dense textured plush or frieze in nylon at 35–50 oz face weight — roughly $3.50–$7 per square foot installed at 2026 Seattle-area market rates. One disclosure up front: we're OC Flooring, a hard-surface company — we don't sell or install carpet — which is exactly why we can rank the options without steering you.

Lynnwood & Snohomish County 2026 market prices (425) 595-1079

Walk into any flooring showroom near Alderwood and you'll face a wall of several hundred carpet samples that are, honestly, about fifteen products wearing different names. We're OC Flooring — a hardwood, vinyl plank, and laminate company working across King and Snohomish County since 2013. We don't sell carpet, but we pull an enormous amount of it out of Lynnwood homes, and homeowners constantly ask what they should put back in the bedrooms. This is the guide we give them: the five constructions that matter, the fiber question underneath, real 2026 market numbers, and an honest map of where carpet wins — and where your money does more as a hardwood floor or vinyl plank floor instead.

Every Carpet Wall Comes Down to a Small Grid

5 × 3

Five constructions times three main fibers (nylon, polyester, triexta) cover nearly every residential carpet sold. Learn the grid and the showroom shrinks.

35–50 oz

the face-weight range worth buying for rooms you use — ounces of fiber per square yard. Below about 30 oz, family traffic flattens carpet fast.

5–15 yrs

a realistic carpet lifespan here — the honest number to weigh against a hardwood floor that gets refinished instead of retired.

Construction is how the yarn is attached and whether the loops are cut — it decides how the carpet looks, feels, and hides wear. Fiber is what the yarn is made of — it decides stain resistance and whether the pile springs back or mats down. Salespeople talk about color and softness; the spec label talks about fiber, face weight, and density, and that's where the lifespan lives.

The 5 Carpet Constructions, Ranked for Real Life

Here's the whole showroom in one table, ranked by how often each construction is the right call in the homes we work in:

ConstructionThe look & feelWhere it belongsThe catch
1. Textured plush (cut pile)Soft, casual; kinked fibers hide footprints and vacuum tracksBedrooms, upstairs halls, family rooms — the defaultQuality varies wildly under one name; buy by the spec label
2. Frieze / twistTightly twisted, slightly shaggy, relaxedThe hardest-working zones: stairs, kids' rooms, busy hallsCasual by nature; crumbs vanish into it
3. Berber / loopWoven, flecked, low and tidyHome offices, finished basementsLoops snag — pet claws, vacuums; big-loop olefin mats
4. Pattern / cut-and-loopSculpted geometric or organic patternsGuest rooms, formal spacesPattern repeats add waste and cost; loops still snag
5. Saxony / plushVelvet-smooth, formal, luxuriousLow-traffic formal rooms, primary bedroomsShows every footprint; mats under real traffic

The short version: for any room with daily traffic, choose a dense textured plush or a frieze. Saxony is lovely in a room mostly walked in slippers, pattern carpet is a style call more than a performance one, and berber is fine — right up until a dog, a cat, or a vacuum finds a loose loop and pulls a run across the floor.

Nylon vs. Polyester vs. Triexta: The Question That Decides Lifespan

Nylon is the fiber to beat. It's the most resilient synthetic in carpet — it springs back after crushing, takes stain treatments well, and it's what we'd put on any staircase if we were buying carpet ourselves. It's also the priciest of the three, which is why so many advertised deals quietly aren't nylon.

Polyester (PET) is the budget fiber — vivid colors, naturally good against spills, noticeably cheaper. Its weakness is resilience: under daily traffic it mats and looks tired years before nylon does. Reasonable in a low-traffic bedroom, poor on halls and stairs. Whole-house carpet advertised near $2 per square foot installed is almost always light polyester.

Triexta is the newer middle path, sold under big-brand stain-resist names. Its stain resistance is built into the fiber rather than sprayed on, it's softer than nylon, and crush resistance lands between polyester and nylon — a genuinely good pick for kids and pets. Brand matters far less than fiber and density; our carpet brand review walks that landscape, but read the fiber line first. (Wool: beautiful, premium-priced, happiest in dry rooms.)

Pick nylon when
  • The carpet covers stairs or a daily-use hall
  • You have dogs, or kids who treat halls as runways
  • You want one carpet to survive 10+ years
  • You'd rather pay once than twice
Polyester or triexta is fine when
  • It's a bedroom or guest room with light traffic
  • Budget must stretch across several rooms today
  • Spills worry you more than crushing — lean triexta
  • You'll update the room within 8 years anyway

An installed price has three parts — carpet (usually $1–$5/sq ft retail), pad, and labor — and stores mix them differently, which is why "free installation" offers are hard to compare. Two defenses: divide any per-yard price by nine, and don't skimp on the pad — a firm 8 lb rebond pad outlasts a squishy 6 lb one. We broke the whole game down in our guide to what carpet should cost in the Seattle market. Stairs, furniture moving, and tear-out add real money — get them itemized in writing.

Where Carpet Still Wins — and Where Lynnwood Homes Regret It

Carpet earns its keep
  • Bedrooms — nothing beats it barefoot in February
  • Upstairs halls and kids' play areas, where quiet matters
  • Media and bonus rooms — it soaks up sound
  • Budgets that must cover every room today
Skip carpet here
  • Entries and mudrooms — 150+ rainy days a year
  • Kitchens, baths, laundry — moisture wins eventually
  • Main floors with dogs — claws, dander, accidents
  • Anywhere you'll sell soon — buyers read it as a project

The pattern that keeps working in Lynnwood: hard surface on the main floor, carpet upstairs where bare feet and quiet matter. Carpet holds what our climate delivers — moisture, grit, dander — which is why allergy and pet households end up happier with floors that wipe clean; our guide to the best flooring for kids and pets goes deep on that trade-off. If you split the house, price the carpet and hard-surface work separately — bundled big-box deals usually price one half poorly.

The Lynnwood Reality Check

Lynnwood's housing spans three carpet-relevant eras. The 1960s–70s ramblers and split-levels around Alderwood Manor, Lake Serene, and Meadowdale often hide their best flooring secret under the existing carpet — more on that check below. The 1980s–90s two-stories near Alderwood Mall were built carpet-everywhere and are now on their second or third replacement cycle — a good moment to break the cycle on the main floor rather than re-buy it. And the townhomes along 196th Street SW near the light rail station that opened in 2024 mostly came with builder-grade floors that owners upgrade within a decade.

Two local notes worth money. If the home has a crawl space — most older Lynnwood ramblers do — look at the old pad when it comes up: moisture marks on the subfloor side are a cheap early warning. And if you're carpeting a rental near the light rail corridor, buy a mid-grade nylon or skip carpet for vinyl plank — turnover traffic kills cheap carpet fastest.

Before You Sign a Carpet Quote: The Two-Minute Closet Check

The most expensive carpet mistake in Lynnwood isn't overpaying per yard — it's re-carpeting over hardwood. In pre-1980 homes here, carpet often covers original oak it has protected for decades. Pull back a corner in a closet and look. If there's wood under there, refinishing it — from $3.99/sq ft with us — lands in the range of good carpet installed and outlives every carpet you'd ever buy. If it's plywood, carry on with bedroom carpet with our blessing. Our walkthrough on removing old carpet shows what tear-out involves.

Lynnwood Carpet Questions, Answered Honestly

What is the best carpet type for a busy family home?
A dense textured plush or a frieze (twist) in nylon, 35–50 oz face weight, over a firm 8 lb pad. It hides footprints and springs back after crushing. Saxony and big-loop berber are the two to avoid in busy rooms.
Is polyester carpet good enough for bedrooms?
Usually, yes. Polyester resists spills well and costs less than nylon; its weakness is matting under heavy traffic, which a bedroom doesn't produce. Save nylon money for halls and stairs, and consider triexta if kids or pets share the room.
What should carpet cost installed in Lynnwood in 2026?
Mid-grade carpet runs roughly $3.50–$7 per square foot installed in the Seattle-area market — carpet at $1–$5 retail plus pad and labor. Below about $2.50 installed is builder grade. Market figures, not our quotes — we don't sell carpet.
Is berber carpet a bad idea with pets?
Big-loop berber is. Claws catch loops, and one pulled loop can zipper a run across the floor. If you love the look, choose a small tight nylon loop or a cut pile with a berber-style fleck instead.
Which numbers on a carpet label actually matter?
Four things: fiber (nylon, triexta, polyester), face weight (35–50 oz for busy rooms), density (part the pile — the harder the backing is to see, the better), and twist level for cut piles (around 5 turns per inch). Those predict lifespan far better than brand names.
Does OC Flooring install carpet?
No — we're a hard-surface company: hardwood installation and refinishing, vinyl plank, and laminate across King and Snohomish County. That's why this guide can be unbiased; we have no carpet to sell you.
Should I check for hardwood before recarpeting an older Lynnwood home?
Yes — it takes two minutes at a closet corner. Pre-1980 Lynnwood homes often have original oak under the carpet, and refinishing costs about the same as good carpet installed while lasting decades longer.
